impact.description: less configuration time through my workflow redesigns

case_study.context: L & S Electric needed a modern desktop app for configuring and controlling its AES-110 and AES-1100 hydro-electric power excitation systems. The users are electrical engineers and field technicians (both inside and outside of L & S Electric, Inc.) working live with power generation equipment, where a misread value or mis-click has drastic consequences. The app had to combine real-time metering, a multi-channel oscilloscope, COMTRADE fault-file analysis, synchroscope and capability curve displays, and automated control sequences.
case_study.my_role: Lead User Experience Designer, Researcher, and Writer

action.action_description: I ran working sessions with L & S electrical engineers to understand how they commission, tune, and troubleshoot excitation systems, and which readings they need side by side during each task. I also shadowed a technician through a commissioning workflow on the legacy tool.

I organized screens into task-based modes (configuration, monitoring, control, fault analysis) so engineers could move between them without losing context. A/B testing with 4 to 5 engineers shaped the navigation.

I designed the auto-control and sequence screens with clear state indicators, confirmation steps for irreversible commands, and consistent placement of critical readings while making sure to follow L & S's own accessibility and HMI standards.
I designed the oscilloscope and COMTRADE views — channel toggles, zoom bands, and RMS/frequency/phase measurement readouts — so engineers could isolate a fault window quickly.
I created a reusable component library (gauges, metering tiles, alarm states) that let development scale consistently.

I reviewed builds with engineers each iteration and refined layouts based on what they actually looked for first, conducting usability walkthroughs at roughly every two to four weeks. I also experimented with field testing during QA testing for AES-110s.

case_study.result: One unified, scalable tool replaced several outdated tools for configuring, monitoring, and analyzing excitation systems. Configuration time decreased by about 50%. Engineers can analyze historical fault events in the same oscilloscope interface they use live, shortening root-cause analysis from hours to minutes. Consistent patterns across all pages reduce training time for new technicians and lower the risk of operator error on live equipment. The product gives L & S a modern, branded software experience to pair with their hardware in customer sales.
case_study.summary: One unified tool replaced several outdated tools for configuring, monitoring, and analyzing excitation systems, and cut configuration time by about 50%.

tldr: L & S Electric needed a modern desktop app for configuring and controlling its AES-110 and AES-1100 hydro-electric power excitation systems.

impact.description: 2nd place in the MSOE AI Club Discovery World hackathon

case_study.context: Discovery World wanted a cost-effective, technology-based way to improve exhibit accessibility. During a 50-hour MSOE AI Club hackathon, our team explored a solution designed to require little effort from visitors.
case_study.my_role: UX researcher and designer; presentation creator.

action.action_description: Visited Discovery World to observe and test existing accessibility tools, consulted stakeholders, and identified visitor needs and underrepresented groups the concept could serve.
Sketched and wireframed a low-cost concept, then prototyped a chatbot that uses Bluetooth repeaters to locate visitors and tailor exhibit information to different ages.
Documented the design process in a presentation and handed the prototype to software engineers for implementation.

case_study.result: The team earned second place with a seamless, cost-effective accessibility concept that was easy to implement and required little to no effort from visitors.
case_study.summary: Designed an accessible, age-aware exhibit chatbot for Discovery World with the MSOE AI Club.

tldr: Designed an accessible, age-aware exhibit chatbot for Discovery World with the MSOE AI Club.

impact.description: One purchase is the liquid soap and the bar. The pump is bought once. Nothing plastic is left to throw away.

case_study.context: Liquid soap is easy and wasteful. A bar is lower waste, and easy to give up on. Hotels throw away half-used bars every day. Over 14 weeks, the brief was a physical product that could be published.

action.action_description: Completed field and competitive research, sketched early concepts, refined the design digitally, and built a rough clay model.
Created 3D models in SolidWorks and Autodesk Fusion 360, inverted the product design into a mold, and 3D-printed the mold.
Collected feedback from peers and professors, tested materials, identified design issues, and refined the product through repeated experiments, including work with flexible TPU molds.

case_study.result: A high-fidelity soap bottle: liquid soap inside, and the bottle itself becomes the bar. The pump is bought once and kept, and the material is recycled hotel soap.
case_study.summary: A hand-soap bottle you use, then wash with. The container is the next bar, so the product leaves no plastic behind.

tldr: A hand-soap bottle you use, then wash with. The container is the next bar, so the product leaves no plastic behind.
Solo work, 14 weeks, from research through a high-fidelity prototype.

sections.label: Background
sections.title: A product that could be published
paragraphs: The brief was a physical product that could be published, taken from an idea to a finished prototype. It was a 14-week industrial design project, and the first one I took on without a team.

sections.label: Problem
sections.title: Convenience that leaves a bottle behind
paragraphs: Liquid soap is easy and wasteful. A bar is lower waste, and easy to give up on. Hotels throw away half-used bars every day.
sections.quote: How do you sell zero waste as the more convenient choice?

sections.label: Process
sections.title: From a sketch to a mold

images.alt: Collage of CAD renders, mold printing, and material tests from the soap bottle process.

subsections.title: Field and competitive research
subsections.body: I started by looking at comparable products and the waste around them, then kept a presentation journal of the decisions as the work moved.

subsections.title: Sketches and a clay model
subsections.body: Rough sketches and a clay model settled the form before it went into CAD.

subsections.title: SolidWorks, then Fusion 360
subsections.body: A convex body fits the hand and still reads as a bar once the liquid is gone. An embossed earth mark carries the brand.

subsections.title: Critique, kept visible
subsections.body: Peers and professors reviewed the work at each pass, and those reviews stayed in the presentation so each decision remained visible.

subsections.title: A mold, then melted hotel soap
subsections.body: I inverted the model into a mold, 3D printed it in flexible TPU, and tested it with melted hotel soap. When consistency, the melt, or the embossing failed, I named the issue, tried a fix, and refined.

sections.label: Final product
sections.title: The bottle is the next bar
sections.quote: Have liquid hand soap inside of the bottle and use the bottle itself once the liquid is gone.

images.alt: The final soap bottle prototype shown from the top, bottom, sides, and an isometric angle.

paragraphs: The pump is bought once and kept. The packaging is compostable. The form is simple enough for a minimalist home, and the soap is gentle enough for sensitive skin.
The prototype is a high-fidelity soap bottle with rounded edges and the earth mark pressed into the face.

sections.label: Impact
sections.title: What the purchase actually is
paragraphs: The customer buys a new soap bottle and keeps the pump. The empty bottle is the next bar, so the refill does not leave a container. The material is soap a hotel would have discarded, and the outer pack can be composted.

stats.label: One purchase is the liquid soap and the bar. The pump is bought once. Nothing plastic is left to throw away.

sections.label: Reflections
sections.title: What I would change next
paragraphs: Making soap is harder than it looks. Learning to 3D print the mold was trial and error, and keeping a journal of the progress mattered.
Next I would use a stovetop to melt the soap, add soap base for a richer consistency, and press the logo with a heated metal stamp. I hoped to fund that next round through my university.
